entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11572"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1-Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:1-21</reference>. The Judgment on Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar; though about to Be Restored after Forty Years, It Was Still to Be in a State of Degradation.</title> <div sID="gen20970" type="x-p"/> This is the last of the world kingdoms against which Ezekiel's prophecies are directed, and occupies the largest space in them, namely, the next four chapters. Though farther off than Tyre, it exercised a more powerful influence on Israel.<div eID="gen20970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11572"/><hi type="bold">2. Pharaoh--</hi>a common name of all the kings of Egypt, meaning "the sun"; or, as others say, a "crocodile," which was worshipped in parts of Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>). Hophra or Apries was on the throne at this time. His reign began prosperously. He took Gaza (<reference osisRef="Jer.47.1">Jr 47:1</reference>) and Zidon and made himself master of Phoenicia and Palestine, recovering much that was lost to Egypt by the victory of Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>), in the fourth year of Jehoiakim [Wilkinson, Ancient Egypt, 1.169]. So proudly secure because of his successes for twenty-five years did he feel, that he said not even a god could deprive him of his kingdom [Herodotus, 2.169]. Hence the appropriateness of the description of him in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>. No mere human sagacity could have enabled Ezekiel to foresee Egypt's downfall in the height of its prosperity. There are four divisions of these prophecies; the first in the tenth year of Ezekiel's captivity; the last in the twelfth. Between the first and second comes one of much later date, not having been given till the twenty-seventh year (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17">Eze 29:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.19">30:19</reference>), but placed there as appropriate to the subject matter. Pharaoh-hophra, or Apries, was dethroned and strangled, and Amasis substituted as king, by Nebuchadnezzar (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">Jr 44:30</reference>). The Egyptian priests, from national vanity, made no mention to Herodotus of the Egyptian loss of territory in Syria through Nebuchadnezzar, of which Josephus tells us, but attributed the change in the succession from Apries to Amasis solely to the Egyptian soldiery. The civil war between the two rivals no doubt lasted several years, affording an opportunity to Nebuchadnezzar of interfering and of elevating the usurper Amasis, on condition of his becoming tributary to Babylon [Wilkinson]. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10-Jer.43.12">Jr 43:10-12</reference>, and see on <reference osisRef="Jer.43.13">Jr 43:13</reference>, for another view of the grounds of interference of Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen20971" type="x-p"/>

So proudly secure because of his successes for twenty-five years did he feel, that he said not even a god could deprive him of his kingdom [Herodotus, 2.169]. Between the first and second comes one of much later date, not having been given till the twenty-seventh year ( Eze 29:17 ; 30:19 ), but placed there as appropriate to the subject matter. Pharaoh-hophra, or Apries, was dethroned and strangled, and Amasis substituted as king, by Nebuchadnezzar (compare Jr 44:30 ). The civil war between the two rivals no doubt lasted several years, affording an opportunity to Nebuchadnezzar of interfering and of elevating the usurper Amasis, on condition of his becoming tributary to Babylon [Wilkinson]. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11574"/><div sID="gen20975" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11574"/><hi type="bold">4. hooks in thy jaws--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Is 37:29</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference>, 2). Amasis was the "hook." In the Assyrian sculptures prisoners are represented with a hook in the underlip, and a cord from it held by the king.<div eID="gen20975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cause ... fish ... stick unto ... scales--</hi>Pharaoh, presuming on his power as if he were God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>, "I have made it"), wished to stand in the stead of God as defender of the covenant-people, his motive being, not love to them, but rivalry with Babylon. He raised the siege of Jerusalem, but it was only for a time (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.6">Eze 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7-Jer.37.10">7-10</reference>); ruin overtook not only them, but himself. As the fish that clung to the horny scales of the crocodile, the lord of the Nile, when he was caught, shared his fate, so the adherents of Pharaoh, lord of Egypt, when he was overthrown by Amasis, should share his fate. <div eID="gen20976" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11575"/><div sID="gen20977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11575"/><hi type="bold">5. wilderness--</hi>captivity beyond thy kingdom. The expression is used perhaps to imply retribution in kind. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11580"/><div sID="gen20987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11580"/><hi type="bold">10. from the tower of Syene--</hi>Grotius translates, "from Migdol (a fortress near Pelusium on the north of Suez) to Syene (in the farthest south)"; that is, from one end of Egypt to the other. So "from Migdol to Syene," <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">Eze 30:6</reference>, Margin. However, English Version rightly refers Syene to Seveneh, that is, Sebennytus, in the eastern delta of the Nile, the capital of the Lower Egyptian kings. The Sebennyte Pharaohs, with the help of the Canaanites, who, as shepherds or merchants, ranged the desert of Suez, extended their borders beyond the narrow province east of the delta, to which they had been confined by the Pharaohs of Upper Egypt. The defeated party, in derision, named the Sebennyte or Lower Egyptians foreigners and shepherd-kings (a shepherd being an abomination in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.46.34">Ge 46:34</reference>). They were really a native dynasty. Thus, in English Version, "Ethiopia" in the extreme south is rightly contrasted with Sebennytus or Syene in the north. <div eID="gen20987" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11581"/><div sID="gen20988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11581"/><hi type="bold">11. forty years--</hi>answering to the forty years in which the Israelites, their former bondsmen, wandered in "the wilderness" (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:5</reference>). Jerome remarks the number forty is one often connected with affliction and judgment. The rains of the flood in forty days brought destruction on the world. Moses, Elias, and the Saviour fasted forty days. The interval between Egypt's overthrow by Nebuchadnezzar and the deliverance by Cyrus, was about forty years. The ideal forty years' wilderness state of social and political degradation, rather than a literal non-passing of man or beast for that term, is mainly intended (so <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.6">Eze 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Is 19:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen20988" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11582"/><div sID="gen20989" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11582"/>12. As Israel passed through a term of wilderness discipline (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.35">Eze 20:35</reference>, &c.), which was in its essential features to be repeated again, so it was to be with Egypt [Fairbairn]. Some Egyptians were to be carried to Babylon, also many "scattered" in Arabia and Ethiopia through fear; but mainly the "scattering" was to be the dissipation of their power, even though the people still remained in their own land. <div eID="gen20989" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11584"/><div sID="gen20991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11584"/><hi type="bold">14. Pathros--</hi>the Thebaid, or Upper Egypt, which had been especially harassed by Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Na 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.10">10</reference>). entries.content_plain: 21. In the evil only, not in the good, was Egypt to be parallel to Israel. The very downfall of Egypt will be the signal for the rise of Israel, because of God's covenant with the latter. I cause the horn of ... Israel to bud-- ( Psa 132:17 ). I will cause its ancient glory to revive: an earnest of Israel's full glory under Messiah, the son of David ( Lu 1:69 ). Even in Babylon an earnest was given of this in Daniel ( Da 6:2 ) and Jeconiah ( Jr 52:31 ). I will give thee ... opening of ... mouth-- When thy predictions shall have come to pass, thy words henceforth shall be more heeded (compare Eze 24:27 ).
